This is a recording of a live AI engineering conference in New York about AI agents, finance, and software. Hi everyone, I'm Ryan, I'm the CEO and one of the co-founders of Val's AI. I'm going to talk a little bit about going from beyond the model card, how evaluations can be used to measure this jagged frontier, a special focus on finance for this audience as well. Yeah, so first off, talking about model cards themselves, we've built some of the most important benchmarks over the last couple of years that the major foundation model labs have included in their model releases. So people I think are familiar with artifacts like this. Last week we have Sundar talking about our Val's index on stage, and then even just yesterday Muse models were citing our finance agent benchmark. You know, it keeps our lives interesting to have to keep re-updating these slides as new models come out. I had to double check level numbers. You can get a sense of how capable a model is for valuable work, but that's actually driving value for a lot of companies. And I think two interesting stats that jump out at me, the groups that are able to actually track AI cost and spend are much, much more likely to have inferior performance, but we also have refined the X-axis. Again, it's not immediately obvious which is number one or will be consistently two or three. In the X-axis, you've got cost. In particular, it's cost per task, not just token and Excel models. You've got cost. In particular, it's cost per task, not just token and Excel models. When we actually build benchmarks, one of the most important things we need to look at is the metric we use to report accuracy. And so you have a different takeaway if you pick a different metric. A lot of benchmarks deal with partial credit, and so what this is answering is, in expectation, if I were to give a question or task to a model, what percentage of the points would I expect to see satisfied by the work output of that model? And then the fully correct answers metric is more looking at, of the percentage of questions that I give to models, what percentage of them will come back perfect? And that's a very different metric. It may mean that a model is very good at producing an incremental response that you can work with to build a better response, but if you were to pass this directly to a client, it would be a coin toss of whether it was meeting all the criteria that you have. And so picking the right metric is very important to accurately representing the performance of the model and actually forming a good intuition of what it can do. There's another three components that we think a lot about, so validity, are you actually evaluating what's going on in the real world? That means are the questions or tasks reflective of actual work going on, or are they contrived? And then are the rubrics actually describing what we're looking for, or the standard of excellence we want to see? Reliability, this is usually a function of the number of tasks or the sample count. A lot of companies, they have maybe five or six samples, and they're kind of vibe checking new models or products as they get access, but it's actually really important to have a rigorous approach and have enough tasks and samples to make sure your repeated runs actually show consistent results. And then last, discriminability. So we don't think it's that valuable to have benchmarks where all models score 100% or all models score 0%. Ideally, we can actually discriminate between models and see what the frontier looks like. In particular, we also want to make sure we're building benchmarks forward looking. So what are the new set of tasks that are even more ambitious than what models can do today to make sure that there's room at the frontier for us to continue to see model progress as they get better? Okay. And then some of the high-level problems that we've seen and I think others can and do run into, the first is that agents solve the test, not the problem. So this is talked a lot about as reward hacking, and we've seen a lot of instances where we'll have a sandbox and models will be run with our model proxy, and sometimes they may try and actually call other models within that proxy to escape the sandbox or make use of the internet. So it's really important to build the containers in a way that you're actually testing for what matters. Can they do the task at hand or are they actually leveraging other tools or maybe even other models to get there? We've also seen this issue in finance in particular where a lot of the times evals are looking at a set of rubrics or items that we want to see included in the response, and so models can hedge and give three possible answers, which has a higher chance of satisfying all the criteria, but in practice, that's way too much. A person does not want to consider three different answers. They just want to get the first answer and have it be right. And so the goal here is to try and build evals that are reflective of the actual work people are doing and the work output they want to see, not to build these contrived evals that the models can actually gain. The second is I think a lot of people are starting to see that the cost of software is coming down and it's actually very, very easy to produce code, but unfortunately, we still see in practice that running evals is incredibly challenging, especially from an infrastructure side of things, and in particular, as we get to longer running agents, it means that it's really important to have infrastructure that can stay consistent over a long period of time and then if interrupted, can be resumed and respunned back up. We have, I think, just recently crossed 6 trillion tokens just in evaluation, so we've run a considerable set of evals and we run everything in as high a degree of parallel as possible. So I think this has really been load tested, but I think other people are going to run to this even on a much smaller scale. And the last is that I think a lot of the existing benchmarks, they deal with a single prompt, single response, but in practice, everything is multi-turn. You have an initial spec which you think covers everything, but then you get questions back or you have additional feedback once something is built, and then it takes more of this iteration to actually drive to the end output. And so I think benchmarks and evals need to actually cover this multi-turn component. That's not going to go away. If you want to look at a case study in particular, when we looked at our team, we did a little token maxing experiment where we got free access to some tools and just gave it to all the engineers, and they really made use of these unlimited tokens, and if we actually look back for that month, we spent $1.5 million worth of tokens. This is like a team of, I think, 10 or 12, so there's roughly 10 times the amount we were spending on salary for tokens in that month, and so that was pretty insane, but we saw great output, and so our goal was to try and maintain the same level of output across all these engineers, but massively cut down on cost, and really our solution to do that was, of course, to build an eval. We built a bunch of tools.
